stem: Which lambda is equivalent to: (int x) => { return x * x; } ?
explanation: Types infer, single parameters need no brackets, and an expression body needs no braces or return. All four spellings in the lesson are one function.
The lambda captured the VARIABLE, not its value at creation. factor is 10 when scale runs, so 100. The most important closure fact.

stem: MakeCounter returns () => ++count where count is a local. After MakeCounter finishes, count:
options: LIVES ON, privately owned by the returned lambda
explanation: Captured locals survive their method. Each MakeCounter() call creates fresh state - two counters count independently. Object-like behaviour, no class.

stem: for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) fs.Add(() => i); Calling all three lambdas afterwards prints:
options: 3, 3, 3 - all captured the ONE loop variable, now 3
explanation: The for-loop trap: one shared i. Copy into a local inside the body (int copy = i) to capture per-iteration. (foreach was fixed in C# 5; for was not.)

stem: Func<int,int> f = static n => n * 2; The static means:
options: The lambda CAPTURES NOTHING - the compiler enforces it
explanation: A guarantee against accidental capture (and its hidden allocation). Try to touch an outer variable and it will not compile.

stem: strings.Select(s => int.Parse(s)) can be shortened to:
explanation: When a lambda only forwards to one method, pass the method group directly - same behaviour, less noise.

stem: A lambda body with an if and two returns requires:
options: A named method - lambdas cannot branch
explanation: n => { if (n < 0) return "neg"; return "pos"; } - braces turn it into a statement body. If it grows past a few lines, extract a named method.

stem: A Dictionary<string, Func<double,double,double>> keyed by "+", "-"... replaces:
options: A switch over operators - and drove the 7.3 command table
explanation: Behaviour stored in collections: operations["*"](12, 4). Adding an operator = adding an entry; the lookup code never changes.

options: Each operator takes a tiny INLINE rule - without lambdas every rule would be a named method three lines away
explanation: words.Where(w => w.Length <= 4).OrderBy(w => w) reads as a sentence precisely because the rules sit inside it.

stem: A lambda that captures locals differs from one that captures nothing in that it:
options: Requires an allocated closure object to carry the captured state
explanation: Captured state lives in a compiler-generated heap object. Usually irrelevant; in a hot path it is 6.2's hidden-allocation story - hence static lambdas.
